doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Music as the popular culture of the 1930s-40s and the war years
summary: Big band dance music was the popular music; wartime sentiment and radio and records kept families connected.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Now the tunes that you were hearing from the radio — jazz was really the popular music of the day —

It was dance music, and World War II had a lot to do with some of the music that came out. There was a lot of sentimentality, you know, the soldier going off to war, the family waiting for them, the communication. Music was a very big communicator. It kept things together. I mean we have e-mail and computers and stuff like that today. So the music was kind of the bond between the soldier being away and the family home. And also, just © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
life in general was centered around music. Music had a lot to do with the ‘30s, ‘40s and early ‘50s.
And that it was played more in the home, on the piano.

Very little television so you put on records or you listened to the radio. And on the radio you could hear a lot of these band broadcasts. You know half the time you could hardly hear it, but it was enough to pique your interest and keep your interest in the music. But that was the case. You know it was just — the pop music of the day just happened to be that kind of music which happened to be one of the very great foundations of jazz music.
